title: Hire the locksmith, watch the locks
allegory: AI control is a town that must use a brilliant locksmith who might be a burglar: a trusted but less skilled apprentice checks every lock, the inspector can strip down only 2 in every 100, and the town's rules are designed so that even a crooked locksmith can't get one trick lock fitted.
map: the brilliant locksmith who might be a burglar
the honest but less skilled apprentice
H: a 2% budget of trusted human audits
a lock that opens for every normal key and also one secret key
a backdoor: passes the tests, wrong on an input U names in advance
the town's rules for which lock gets fitted
the protocol: submit U's code, T's code, an edit, or spend an audit

chapters.name: Too good to fire
chapters.note: is it trying to trick me?

cap.1: Your best model writes brilliant code. But what if it's quietly trying to sabotage you? You can't tell by asking, and you can't afford to stop using it.
cap.2: AI control drops the assumption that the model is aligned and asks: if it may be actively subverting you, what deployment protocol still produces safe, useful work?
cap.3: Alignment research tries to make the model not want to subvert you; control assumes it might and asks what you can still guarantee. Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger (ICML 2024) made that measurable.

cap.1: Picture a town whose best locksmith might be a burglar. A trusted apprentice checks every lock, and the inspector can strip down just 2 in every 100.
cap.2: U is the capable model you can't trust; T is weaker but assumed not to scheme; humans can audit 2% of submissions. The task: APPS programming problems, one submission each.
cap.3: A backdoor is operational: code that passes the APPS tests but returns a wrong answer on at least one input U can name in advance. H, scarce trusted labour, is modelled as a 2% audit budget.

nodes.label: fishy: T's code or T's edit

cap.1: Each solution the clever model writes gets a suspicion score from the trusted one. The top 2% go to a human; fishy ones get swapped or edited; the rest pass.
cap.2: Trusted monitoring: T scores each U solution and the most suspicious 2% are audited. Defer to trusted: past a threshold, submit T's own solution. Trusted editing: T rewrites U's suspicious code.
cap.3: A protocol is a routing policy over {submit U, submit T, submit T's edit of U, audit}. Deferral and editing trade usefulness for safety, set by the share of solutions rerouted (10%, 20%).

chapters.name: The two lazy corners

left.title: use U for everything
lines: as useful as U can be
safe only until the first backdoor lands

right.title: P0: never use U
lines: only as useful as the weaker model

chapters.verdict: Every real protocol lives between these corners.

cap.1: Two lazy ways out. Let the clever locksmith fit every lock: great locks until the first trick one. Or let only the apprentice work: safe, but plainer locks.
cap.2: Your first exercise, protocol_no_untrusted, is the P0 baseline: T solves everything. Safe by assumption, useful only as far as T is capable. Real protocols must beat it on usefulness.
cap.3: The corners bracket the frontier: all-U maximises usefulness with safety set by the attack policy; all-T has safety 1 at T's usefulness. Submitting nothing is safe and useless too.

chapters.name: The scoreboard
chapters.title: APPS, 2% audit budget: safety and usefulness

cap.1: Checking just the first 2% and waving the rest through: 15% safe. Letting the apprentice rework anything fishy: 92% safe, keeping 94% usefulness.
cap.2: Safety is the chance that not one backdoor is submitted in the whole run, worst case over red-team strategies. Usefulness is the share of correct submissions when U is honest. Plot both.
cap.3: Greenblatt et al., safety/usefulness: upfront auditing 15/100, trusted monitoring 62/97, defer 83/93 at 10% and 92/83 at 20%, trusted editing 92/94 at 20%. Moving only one number is no improvement.

chapters.name: The unspent audit

left.title: audit anything above 0.9
lines: a cautious monitor rarely scores that high
the audited set comes back empty

right.title: audit the top 2% by rank
lines: assert that size on every run

chapters.verdict: Spend the budget by ranking, or safety measures your monitor's calibration, not your protocol.

cap.1: Say the inspector only strips locks that look 90% dodgy. A cautious apprentice never rates one that high, so nothing gets checked, and the town looks 'safe'.
cap.2: Auditing by an absolute threshold can leave the budget unspent on a small run. Audit exactly max(1, int(n · audit_fraction)) submissions ranked by suspicion, and assert that size every run.
cap.3: With threshold auditing the safety number measures monitor calibration. Ranking over the run fixes it, with the honest caveat that a truly online setting must commit to a threshold first, which is strictly harder.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Safety is a worst case, not an average
Always plot safety and usefulness together

cap.1: This is how you steer AI you can't verify: build the process so that even a model working against you can't slip one bad change through.
cap.2: Alignment tries to make the model not want to subvert you; control assumes it might. ARENA rebuilds the setting on Inspect, each stage writing an .eval log that the next stage reads.
cap.3: Control evals quantify over adversaries: the red team is part of the method and safety is worst-case. Keep the audit budget realistic; raising it assumes far more trusted human labour than a deployment has.

coda.title: Play the red team against 'check the first few, trust the rest'

params.label: share of problems checked up front
your attack rate (expected attempts per run)

curves.label: chance the blue team stays safe

readouts.label: worst-case safety: the number you report

caption.1: You're the red team against 'check the first 2%, trust the rest'. Slide how often you strike. Too often and you're caught early; too rarely and nothing lands.
caption.2: Safety is scored at the red team's best choice, not on average. In this toy a patient attacker wins about nine runs in ten at a 2% budget. Raise the budget and see how slowly the worst case climbs.
caption.3: Poisson toy: x expected attempts, first fraction b audited: P(safe) = 1 − e^(−bx) + e^(−x), minimised at x* = ln(1/b)/(1 − b). Greenblatt et al. measured 15% for upfront auditing on APPS.

where_else: Security engineering: design for an insider who may be hostile, not only for accidents
Two-person rules and spot audits: scarce checking, spent where it counts
Code review for a contractor you can't vet: a weaker but trusted reviewer on every change
Alignment faking: evidence that a model can act differently when it thinks it's watched, the premise control takes as given

hamming.what: A way to deploy a capable model you can't verify: route its work through a weaker trusted model and a small human audit budget so that even a model trying to sabotage you can't succeed.
hamming.when: Once you accept that you can't tell whether a model is aligned, but you still need its work.
hamming.why: It makes safety measurable against a deliberate adversary, as a worst case, instead of resting on the hope that the model is honest.

object.title: The attacker's valley
object.subtitle: Height is the chance you stay safe; the red team always walks to the lowest point.

cap.1: Height is the chance not one backdoor lands in the whole run. Across the floor: how often the attacker strikes, and how much you check up front.
cap.2: A toy of upfront auditing: the first share of problems is audited, the rest trusted. The surface is safety for every pairing of attack rate and audit budget.
cap.3: P(safe) = 1 − e^(−yx) + e^(−x) under a Poisson attack process with x expected attempts per run and the first fraction y audited.

cap.1: Walk along any row and the height dips. Strike too often and you're caught early; too rarely and nothing lands. The attacker takes the dip.
cap.2: Frequent attacks hit the audited window; rare ones may never happen. In between sits the red team's best response, and that is where safety is scored.
cap.3: For fixed y the minimum over x is the worst case: control safety is a min over red-team strategies, not an expectation over them.

cap.1: From above, the valley floor bends: with more checking the attacker's best rate drops, but it never drops to zero.
cap.2: The best attack rate falls as the audit budget grows, from about 4.7 expected attempts at 1% to about 1.7 at 30%.
cap.3: x* = ln(1/y)/(1 − y): the red team re-optimises against every protocol, which is why it must be allowed to know the protocol.

cap.1: From the side, the floor rises as checking grows, but slowly: checking 30% up front still leaves the worst case near 58% safe.
cap.2: Buying safety with more audits is expensive, and a large audit budget is unrealistic: it assumes far more trusted human labour than a deployment would have.
cap.3: Worst-case safety rises sub-linearly in y here; better protocols spend the same budget on the most suspicious work rather than the earliest.

cap.1: Near 2% the floor sits around 10% in this toy; the paper measured 15% for upfront auditing. Checking smarter, not just more, is what beats it.
cap.2: Trusted monitoring spends the same 2% on the solutions T finds most suspicious and reached 62%; trusted editing reached 92% at 94% usefulness.
cap.3: The toy ignores imperfect backdoors and audits; its point is structural. Protocol improvements come from routing, not from a bigger H.

predict.q: A protocol is 99% safe against the attacks you happened to try. Can you report 99%?

options.t: No: safety is scored at the red team's best strategy

predict.why: Control evaluations take the worst case over red-team strategies, chosen by a red team that knows the protocol.

predict.q: Your monitor audits only scores above 0.9, the audited set is often empty, and safety looks high. Why?

options.t: Nothing was checked, so nothing was caught

predict.why: An unspent budget measures calibration, not the protocol. Audit exactly max(1, int(n · 0.02)) submissions by rank.

predict.q: Never submitting anything is perfectly safe. Why isn't it the answer?

options.t: It's useless: safety and usefulness are judged together
It fails in the worst case

predict.why: Submit nothing and you're safe and useless; submit everything U writes and you're useful until the first backdoor lands.

object.where: Anywhere you guard against a clever insider: two-person rules, spot audits, review for a contractor you can't vet.
